key_concepts: [url]Blender Low Poly Character: PS1 Style Modeling for Beginners^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uIHuqFLa_X0[/url]

content: PlayStation 1 models were created with overlapping sections and are relatively straightforward to produce.
Start with a new scene. [k]A,Del[/k] to remove the default camera, cube, and light. Add your reference image in both front and side views (Image 1).

image.caption: Image 1 - Positioning reference images

content: [k]Shift-A > Mesh > Cube[/k] to add a cube to the scene, move it up ([k]G,Z[/k]) to the head and [k]S[/k] to scale it down to a similar width (Image 2). [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode, [k]Ctrl-R[/k] to add a Loop Cut down the middle, delete the left half, and add a Mirror Modifier across the x-axis (Image 3). Begin shaping the head, moving the top vertices up and out (Image 4) and the bottom vertices in and down (Image 5).

image.caption: Image 2 - Adding a cube to the scene, moving it up to the head and scaling it down to a similar width
Image 3 - Going into Edit Mode, adding a Loop Cut down the middle, deleting the left half, and adding a Mirror Modifier across the x-axis
Image 4 - Beginning to shape the head by moving the top vertices up and out
Image 5 - Moving the bottom vertices in and down

content: Add a horizontal Loop Cut and drag the outer edge out to the ear (Image 6). Drag the top edge inwards if it stands out too far now that the cheekbones are shaped (Image 7). Add a Loop Cut to the top of the head and drag the outer edge out (Image 8), and add another Loop Cut to the bottom half and line its vertices up with the nose and cheeks (Image 9).

image.caption: Image 6 - Adding a horizontal Loop Cut and dragging the outer edge out to the ear
Image 7 - Dragging the top edge inwards if it stands out too far now that the cheekbones are shaped
Image 8 - Adding a Loop Cut to the top of the head and dragging the outer edge out
Image 9 - Adding another Loop Cut to the bottom half and lining its vertices up with the nose and cheeks

content: [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View and grab the top vertices and [k]G,Y[/k] to move them in along the y-axis (Image 10). Going clockwise around the head, shape the remaining vertices along the contours of the head (Image 11). Do the same thing for the front vertices (Image 12). Grab the vertices by the forehead and [k]R[/k] to rotate them to match the slope (Image 13). Add a Loop Cut down the middle (Image 14).

image.caption: Image 10 - Going to Side View and grabbing the top vertices and moving them in along the y-axis
Image 11 - Going clockwise around the head, shaping the remaining vertices along the contours of the head
Image 12 - Doing the same thing for the front vertices
Image 13 - Grabbing the vertices by the forehead and rotating them to match the slope
Image 14 - Adding a Loop Cut down the middle

content: Select the front vertices (Image 15). [k]Numpad7[/k] into Top View and [k]G,G[/k] to slide them in along the y- and x-axes to round out the head (Image 16). Do the same with the back vertices (Image 17). In the Side View move some vertices in the top (Image 18) and bottom (Image 19) to round out the shape and better match the reference image. In Front View, you may need to make some adjustments for the jaw line (Image 20) and eyebrow (Image 21).

image.caption: Image 15 - Selecting the front vertices
Image 16 - Going to Top View and sliding the vertices in along the y- and x-axes to round out the head
Image 17 - Doing the same with the back vertices
Image 18 - Moving some vertices in the top in Side View to round out the shape and better match the reference image
Image 19 - Moving some vertices in the bottom in Side View to round out the shape and better match the reference image
Image 20 - Making adjustments for the jaw line in Front View
Image 21 - Making adjustments for the eyebrow in Front View

content: [k]3[/k] into Face Mode and select the bottom face of the head. [k]E[/k] to extrude it down to about the collar bone (Image 22). We do this so that the neck will overlap with the chest. Go into Side View and [k]S[/k] to [k]S,Y[/k], [k]G,Y[/k] the bottom faces and move them back to keep the contours of the neck (Image 23). Add a Loop Cut to the neck, and then in Front and Side Views, [k]S,X[/k], [k]S,Y[/k] to scale it in to match the neck shape (Image 24).

image.caption: Image 22 - Going into Face Mode, selecting the bottom face of the head and extruding it down to about the collar bone
Image 23 - Going into Side View, scaling and moving the bottom faces back to keep the contours of the neck
Image 24 - Adding a Loop Cut to the neck and then scaling it in the x- and y-axes in Front and Side Views to match the neck shape

section.header: Modeling the Nose and Ear Details
content: Go to Front View and add a vertical Loop Cut, moving it in towards the edge of the nose (Image 25). Select the vertex by the top of the nose and [k]G,G[/k] to slide it in (Image 26). Grab the face by the nose and [k]E[/k] to extrude it out (Image 27). Select the front face the nose and [k]G[/k], [k]S[/k], [k]R[/k] to grab, scale, and rotate the tip of the nose until you have a good shape (Image 28). Grab the two vertices under the nose and move them as well to help the shape (Image 29).

image.caption: Image 25 - Going to Front View and adding a vertical Loop Cut, moving it in towards the edge of the nose
Image 26 - Selecting the vertex by the top of the nose and sliding it in
Image 27 - Grabbing the face by the nose and extruding it out
Image 28 - Selecting the front face of the nose and grabbing, scaling, and rotating the tip of the nose until achieving a good shape
Image 29 - Grabbing the two vertices under the nose and moving them to help the shape

content: Go to Side View and select the two faces around the ear and [k]I[/k] to inset faces for the ear (Image 30). [k]E[/k] to extrude them out (Image 31) and shape them as best you can (Image 32).

image.caption: Image 30 - Going to Side View, selecting the two faces around the ear and insetting faces for the ear
Image 31 - Extruding them out
Image 32 - Shaping them as best you can

content: Add a Cube to the scene and give it a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis with clipping enabled (Image 33). Add a vertical Loop Cut and line up the top inside vertices where the neck meets the torso (Image 34). Move the outside vertices to where the shoulder begins (Image 35). Make a horizontal Loop Cut lined up with the arm socket (Image 36). Grab the bottom vertices and move them up to above the belly button and then [k]S,X[/k] to scale them in (Image 37). Make another horizontal Loop Cut towards the bottom of the rib cage and again [k]S,X[/k] to bring them in (Image 38).

image.caption: Image 33 - Adding a Cube to the scene and giving it a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis with clipping enabled
Image 34 - Adding a vertical Loop Cut and lining up the top inside vertices where the neck meets the torso
Image 35 - Moving the outside vertices to where the shoulder begins
Image 36 - Making a horizontal Loop Cut lined up with the arm socket
Image 37 - Grabbing the bottom vertices and moving them up to above the belly button and then scaling them in
Image 38 - Making another horizontal Loop Cut towards the bottom of the rib cage and scaling them in

content: [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View and move the top edge to match the image reference (Image 39). Position the next edge around the chest and back (Image 40). Move down to the next edge and place them under the pectoral (Image 41). Select the bottom edge and [k]G,Y[/k], [k]S,Y[/k] it into position (Image 42). [k]Ctrl-R[/k] to add a vertical Loop Cut to the side (Image 43). In Top View, [k]G,G[/k] the front and back edges to round out the torso (Image 44).

image.caption: Image 39 - Going to Side View and moving the top edge to match the image reference
Image 40 - Positioning the next edge around the chest and back
Image 41 - Moving down to the next edge and placing them under the pectoral
Image 42 - Selecting the bottom edge and moving and scaling it into position
Image 43 - Adding a vertical Loop Cut to the side
Image 44 - Going to Top View and sliding the front and back edges to round out the torso

content: Add a new cube for the hips and give it a Mirror Modifier (Image 45). Go into Edit Mode and shape the hips from the front (Image 46) and the side (Image 47). Add a Loop Cut in the y-axis (Image 48) and then [k]S,Y[/k] the outer hip face to add some roundness (Image 49).

image.caption: Image 45 - Adding a new cube for the hips and giving it a Mirror Modifier
Image 46 - Going into Edit Mode and shaping the hips from the front
Image 47 - Shaping the hips from the side
Image 48 - Adding a Loop Cut in the y-axis
Image 49 - Scaling the outer hip face in the y-axis to add some roundness

content: Add a Loop Cut in the x-axis (Image 50) and then adjust that edge to match the contours of the reference image (Image 51). If you want, you can add another Loop Cut in the y-axis and then adjust that edge to match the contours of the lower back (Image 52). In Top View, add a Loop Cut in the x-axis (Image 53) and then select the Edge Loops on either side and [k]G,G[/k] to Edge Slide them in to round out the hips (Image 54).

image.caption: Image 50 - Adding a Loop Cut in the x-axis
Image 51 - Adjusting that edge to match the contours of the reference image
Image 52 - Adding another Loop Cut in the y-axis and adjusting that edge to match the contours of the lower back
Image 53 - Going to Top View and adding a Loop Cut in the x-axis
Image 54 - Selecting the Edge Loops on either side and Edge Sliding them in to round out the hips

content: Add a cube to the scene and move it up to the shoulder area (Image 55). [k]R[/k], [k]G[/k], [k]S,Z[/k] until is approximates the upper arm (Image 56). Rotate around to Side View and rotate and move the arm into position matching the reference image (Image 57). Go into Top View and make sure it's not too far off from the shoulder area (Image 58).

image.caption: Image 55 - Adding a cube to the scene and moving it up to the shoulder area
Image 56 - Rotating, moving, and scaling it in the z-axis until it approximates the upper arm
Image 57 - Rotating around to Side View and rotating and moving the arm into position matching the reference image
Image 58 - Going to Top View and making sure it's not too far off from the shoulder area

content: Go into Edit Mode, select the back face and scale it up and move it into to overlap the torso (Image 59). Add a Loop Cut near the top of the arm (Image 60). Select the outer edge and move it up to create a curve for the shoulder (Image 61). Move the opposite edge back (Image 62). Scale in the bottom edge for the elbow joint (Image 63).

image.caption: Image 59 - Going into Edit Mode, selecting the back face and scaling it up and moving it to overlap the torso
Image 60 - Adding a Loop Cut near the top of the arm
Image 61 - Selecting the outer edge and moving it up to create a curve for the shoulder
Image 62 - Moving the opposite edge back
Image 63 - Scaling in the bottom edge for the elbow joint

content: In Object Mode, [k]Shift-D[/k] the upper arm and move it down and rotate it to match the lower arm (Image 64). Select the upper arm again, go into Edit Mode, and move the lower face down to the lower arm (Image 65). Add one more Loop Cut, rotate and scale it out to add some thickness for the biceps and triceps (Image 66). In Object Mode, Front View, move the lower arm into the correct position (Image 67).

image.caption: Image 64 - Going to Object Mode, duplicating the upper arm and moving it down and rotating it to match the lower arm
Image 65 - Selecting the upper arm again, going into Edit Mode, and moving the lower face down to the lower arm
Image 66 - Adding one more Loop Cut, rotating and scaling it out to add some thickness for the biceps and triceps
Image 67 - Going to Object Mode and Front View and moving the lower arm into the correct position

content: In Edit Mode, select the edge loops individually and scale, move, rotate them into place (Image 68). In order to round out the forearm, add an Edge Loop (Image 69). Select the edges on the outside of the forearm and [k]G,G[/k] to Edge Slide them in (Image 70). Repeat for the edges on the inside of the forearm (Image 71).

image.caption: Image 68 - Going into Edit Mode, selecting the edge loops individually and scaling, moving, and rotating them into place
Image 69 - Adding an Edge Loop to round out the forearm
Image 70 - Selecting the edges on the outside of the forearm and Edge Sliding them in
Image 71 - Repeating for the edges on the inside of the forearm

content: Add a cube to the scene and move it up to the hand area and scale it down nice and thin (Image 72). Move around to Side View and bring it into position (Image 73). Add a Loop Cut down the middle and adjust the shape (Image 74). Go to the Front View and re-position (Image 75).

image.caption: Image 72 - Adding a cube to the scene, moving it up to the hand area and scaling it down nice and thin
Image 73 - Moving around to Side View and bringing it into position
Image 74 - Adding a Loop Cut down the middle and adjusting the shape
Image 75 - Going to Front View and re-positioning

content: Extrude the front face down, rotate it, and scale in the x-axis, to make a knuckle (Image 76). Extrude, rotate, and scale to the end of the hand (Image 77). To make a thumb, select the outer face (Image 78) and extrude it out to the first knuckle, rotating and scaling into position (Image 79). Continue extruding, rotating, and scaling for the end of the thumb (Image 80).

image.caption: Image 76 - Extruding the front face down, rotating it, and scaling in the x-axis to make a knuckle
Image 77 - Extruding, rotating, and scaling to the end of the hand
Image 78 - Selecting the outer face to make a thumb
Image 79 - Extruding it out to the first knuckle, rotating and scaling into position
Image 80 - Continuing to extrude, rotate, and scale for the end of the thumb

content: [k]Shift-D[/k] the upper arm and move it down to the upper leg, rotating it into position (Image 81). Move it into position from the Side View (Image 82). If the leg is at an awkward angle, rotate it in the z-axis, and then move the vertices into position from the front (Image 83) and the side (Image 84).

image.caption: Image 81 - Duplicating the upper arm and moving it down to the upper leg, rotating it into position
Image 82 - Moving it into position from the Side View
Image 83 - Rotating the leg in the z-axis if at an awkward angle, and then moving the vertices into position from the front
Image 84 - Moving the vertices into position from the side

content: Add a Loop Cut (Image 85). round out the thigh by Edge Sliding the outer (Image 86) and inner edges (Image 87). Select the top loop and move it up into the hip so there is overlap (Image 88).

image.caption: Image 85 - Adding a Loop Cut
Image 86 - Rounding out the thigh by Edge Sliding the outer edges
Image 87 - Rounding out the thigh by Edge Sliding the inner edges
Image 88 - Selecting the top loop and moving it up into the hip so there is overlap

content: Duplicate the upper leg and move it down (Image 89). In Edit Mode, move the Edge Loops around until they match the reference image from the front (Image 90) and side (Image 91).

image.caption: Image 89 - Duplicating the upper leg and moving it down
Image 90 - Going into Edit Mode and moving the Edge Loops around until they match the reference image from the front
Image 91 - Moving the Edge Loops around until they match the reference image from the side

content: Add a Cube to the scene and [k]G,Z,1[/k] to move it up above the origin (Image 92). Change the Transform Pivot Point to the 3D Cursor and scale and move the cube along the x-axis into position (Image 93). Extrude the top and front faces to make a blocky boot shape (Image 94). Change the Transform Pivot Point back to Median Point, add a Loop Cut at the front of the foot and shape it from the side (Image 95). In Top View, select the front face of the foot, scale in the x-axis, rotate slightly, and re-position to add a little bit of a curve to the foot (Image 96).

image.caption: Image 92 - Adding a Cube to the scene and moving it up above the origin
Image 93 - Changing the Transform Pivot Point to the 3D Cursor and scaling and moving the cube along the x-axis into position
Image 94 - Extruding the top and front faces to make a blocky boot shape
Image 95 - Changing the Transform Pivot Point back to Median Point, adding a Loop Cut at the front of the foot and shaping it from the side
Image 96 - Going to Top View, selecting the front face of the foot, scaling in the x-axis, rotating slightly, and re-positioning to add a little bit of a curve to the foot

content: Go around the model making any touch-ups and ensuring all body parts overlap. Add a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis to one limb, using the torso as the Mirror Object (Image 97). Select all the remaining limb parts and [k]Ctrl-L,P[/k] to copy the modifier (Image 98). Hide the reference images and admire your work.

image.caption: Image 97 - Adding a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis to one limb, using the torso as the Mirror Object
Image 98 - Selecting all the remaining limb parts and copying the modifier

key_concepts: [url]Blender Tutorial: Texture Painting for PS1 Characters (Beginner Friendly)^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R76e7CQ3D7s&list=PLn3ukorJv4vuElMnRXKXos4yJZpfTYNLP&index=2[/url]

section.header: Preparing for Texturing: UV Editing Workspace
content: Open the UV Editing workspace (Image 1). [k]A[/k] to select all vertices; you should notice that only the vertices for the last active mesh are selected and appear in the UV workspace (Image 2). We want unwrap the mesh for the entire character. [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode and [k]A[/k] to select all parts (Image 3); you will see the UV map update to show all faces.

image.caption: Image 1 - Opening the UV Editing workspace
Image 2 - Selecting all vertices and noticing that only the vertices for the last active mesh are selected and appear in the UV workspace
Image 3 - Going into Edit Mode and selecting all parts to update the UV map to show all faces

content: Back in Edit Mode, [k]A[/k] to select all faces (Image 4). [k]UV > Smart UV Project[/k] to begin open the Smart UV Project dialog (Image 5). Set the island setting to 0.01 and press [k]Unwrap[/k] (Image 6). In the UV Map, all faces have now been projected out (Image 7).

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces
Image 5 - Opening the Smart UV Project dialog
Image 6 - Setting the island setting to 0.01 and pressing Unwrap
Image 7 - Viewing all faces now projected out in the UV Map

content: Examines the angles between the selected faces, cuts them along any sharp edges, then projects each separated group of faces along its average normal and lays it out on the UV map. You can also set up seams for additional cutting. This is a good method for, say, mechanical objects or architecture.
The [url]Adjust Last Operation^^https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/interface/undo_redo.html#bpy-ops-screen-redo-last[/url] panel allows fine control over how the mesh is unwrapped:

The maximum allowed angle between the normals of adjacent faces before they’re split off from each other. A low limit will create lots of small UV islands with little distortion, while a high limit will create a few large islands with potentially more distortion.
The meaning of the [i]Island Margin[/i] parameter, which determines the size of the empty space between UV islands.
The [i]Island Margin[/i] is a more or less arbitrary measure with no direct relation to the sizes of the UV islands or the texture.
As above, but without the internally calculated scaling factor.

The [i]Island Margin[/i] is a fraction of the UV unit square. This means that, if you have a 1024x1024 texture and set the [i]Island Margin[/i] to 1/1024, each UV island will have a margin of 1 pixel around it (and islands will be no closer than 2 pixels to each other).
Automatically rotate to avoid wasting space.
Rotate islands to be aligned horizontally.
Rotate islands to be aligned vertically.
How much empty space to leave between islands. Controlled by [i]Margin Method[/i].

With a value of 0, the projection vector of each face group is simply the average of its face normals. With a value of 1, it’s an average that’s weighted using the faces’ areas. Other values blend between the two.
Adjusts the UV mapping to account for the aspect ratio of the image associated with the material. This ensures that UVs are scaled correctly when unwrapping onto non-square textures.

For this option to work, the mesh must have a material with an [url]Image Texture node^^https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/textures/image.html[/url], and this node must be selected in the [url]Shader Editor^^https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/editors/shader_editor.html[/url].
Stretches the resulting UV map to fill the complete texture.

Open the Texture Paint workspace (Image 9). Immediately you will notice part of the mesh is purple; that indicates that is the active object, and that no texture is assigned (Image 10). On the left you will the see the Image Editor showing the UVs have been projected onto an image (Image 11). The cursor has also changed to a circle where paint can be applied. If you try to paint an error message will appear; that is because no texture has been assigned to the mesh (Image 12).

image.caption: Image 9 - Opening the Texture Paint workspace
Image 10 - Noticing part of the mesh is purple, indicating it is the active object with no texture assigned
Image 11 - Seeing the Image Editor on the left showing the UVs projected onto an image
Image 12 - Trying to paint and seeing an error message appear because no texture has been assigned to the mesh

content: Go to the top right corner of the left panel; you will know you are in the right spot when the cursor changes to cross hairs. Pull the window down to create a new panel on top (Image 13). Change the editor type for the new panel from Image Editor to Shader Editor (Image 14). You can press [k]N[/k] to get rid of the side panel that appears (Image 15).

image.caption: Image 13 - Going to the top right corner of the left panel and pulling the window down to create a new panel on top
Image 14 - Changing the editor type for the new panel from Image Editor to Shader Editor
Image 15 - Pressing N to get rid of the side panel that appears

section.header: Setting up the Material and Texture Slot
content: At the top go to [k]Texture Slots > + > Base Color[/k] (Image 16). Give the color a good name, in true PS1 fashion reduce the size to 512px, select the skin color you like, and turn off alpha (Image 17). In the Shader Editor there are now 3 nodes created for the texture (Image 18), update the Roughness and Specular for a skin tone if you would like. Below that in the Image Editor you will see the UV texture now has the color applied (Image 19). In the 3D Viewport, the Texture Paint workspace defaults to Solid Mode, change this to Material Preview (Image 20). We can see the texture is only applied to the active object, not all parts of the mesh. Go to Object Mode (Image 21). Select all objects with the object with the material as the active object, [k]Ctrl-L,M[/k] to link materials (Image 22).

image.caption: Image 16 - Going to Texture Slots and adding a Base Color
Image 17 - Giving the color a good name, reducing the size to 512px, selecting a skin color, and turning off alpha
Image 18 - Seeing 3 nodes created for the texture in the Shader Editor and updating the Roughness and Specular for a skin tone
Image 19 - Seeing the UV texture with the color applied in the Image Editor below
Image 20 - Changing the 3D Viewport from Solid Mode to Material Preview in the Texture Paint workspace
Image 21 - Going to Object Mode and noticing the texture is only applied to the active object
Image 22 - Selecting all objects with the material object as the active object and linking materials

content: Go into Texture Paint Mode (Image 23). We can start painting, but if you want to change the current active object in Texture Paint Mode, press [k]Alt-Q[/k]. Go to the Color Picker on the right (Image 24). Click on the left half of the color bar to change your primary color (Image 25).

image.caption: Image 23 - Going into Texture Paint Mode
Image 24 - Going to the Color Picker on the right
Image 25 - Clicking on the left half of the color bar to change the primary color

content: [K]Alt-Q[/k] over the torso to select it and [k]LMB[/k] to start painting (Image 26). On the right, go to [k]Color Palette > New > +[/k] to add the current color to the palette (Image 27). You can use the palette to quickly swap between colors. Paint the torso and upper arms green for a sweater (Image 28). If you need to change the size of your brush, [k]F[/k] to increase or decrease the size (Image 29). In the Image Editor, if you want to select a color from the image, hover the color you want and press [k]Shift-X[/k] to choose that color (Image 30). Make a dark blue color for the pants and dark brown for the shoes and paint those parts (Image 31).

image.caption: Image 26 - Clicking Alt-Q over the torso to select it and starting to paint
Image 27 - Going to Color Palette and adding the current color to the palette
Image 28 - Painting the torso and upper arms green for a sweater
Image 29 - Using F to increase or decrease the size of the brush
Image 30 - Hovering over a color in the Image Editor and pressing Shift-X to select that color
Image 31 - Making a dark blue color for the pants and dark brown for the shoes and painting those parts

content: Prepare for rigging by [k]Shift-S,W[/k] to move the 3D Cursor to the World Origin (Image 1). This will make positioning the righ easier. Make sure Rigify is activated. Go to [k]Edit > Preferences[/k] to open the Preferences dialog and under Add-Ons search for Rigify and enable it (Image 2). [k]Shift-A > Armature > Rigify Meta-Rigs > Human[/k] to add the rig to the scene (Image 3). It will be hard to see, so with the armature selected, go to the Data tab on the right, open Viewport Display and check In Front (Image 4).

image.caption: Image 1 - Opening the UV Editing workspace

content: It is easy to mess up; frequently go into Object Mode and click the Generate Rig button (Image 5). If you messed up, you might get an error message such as [k]blender RIGIFY ERROR: Bone 'thigh.L': Input to rig type must be a chain of at least 4 bones. Incorrect armature for type 'limb_rigs'[/k]; in that case undo you last changes and start again.

image.caption: Image 1 - Opening the UV Editing workspace

section.header: Matching the Bones to the Character Mesh
content: In Object Mode, select the armature and scale it to about the right size (Image 5). [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode and turn on the X-symmetry to apply changes to both sides of the armature (Image 6). Zoom in on the shoulder, [k]Shift-RMB[/k] to move the 3D cursor to the shoulder, and change the Transform Pivot Point to the 3D Cursor (Image 7). This will make it easier to rotate bones. Select the bones of the arm and hand and [k]R[/k] to rotate it into place (Image 8). Change the Pivot Point back to Median Point (Image 9) and move the hand and elbow joints into better position (Image 10). [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View and move the arm bones into position (Image 11). Our model only has a thumb and a paw; not all finger bones are needed. Keep the middle finger bones, but select all other finger bones and [k]X,B[/k] to remove them (Image 12). We need to position the fingers, but this can be awkward. Turn on Snapping and set the Snap Base to Volume (Image 13). This will snap the bones to the volume of the mesh.

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces

content: Start at the bottom and move the bones of the middle finger into place (Image 14). Sometimes when you go to move a bone you could accidentally disconnect them (Image 15). In that case, [k]Ctrl-Z[/k] to undo and then box select the joint area and then move into position (Image 16). The last bone of the finger is actually the hand bone; move it towards the wrist (Image 17).

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces

content: Move the thumb bones in place as well, remembering that the last bone is also the hand bone (Image 18).

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces

content: Turn off snapping and go into Side View (Image 19). Move the knee bone, ankle bone, and toe into position (Image 20). Move the heel bone to just the bottom corner (Image 21). In Front View, [k]G,X[/k] to move the foot bones over (Image 22). Grab the foot roll bone and scale it up to be as wide as the foot (Image 23). Go up and move the knee and hip joints into position (Image 24).

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces

content: Select all the face bones (Image 25) and delete them. Delete the ear bones as well (Image 26). [k]Alt-LMB[/k] on the head bone and you will see there is a hidden bone there called face (Image 27). Delete that last one (Image 28).

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces

content: Move around the model, making any final adjustments and save your work (Image 29).

image.caption: Image 4 - Going back into Edit Mode and selecting all faces

content: Go into Object Mode and with the armature selected, [k]N[/k] to bring up the Item properties window (Image 30). We see the scale is off, so [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale (Image 31). Press the [k]Generate Rig[/k] button to generate (Image 32). If you go to the outliner there are now two objects: metarig which was the original bones and rig which is the rig controls; hide or delete the metarig (Image 33).

Select all mesh objects and the rig, making sure the rig is the active object and [k]Ctrl-P > With Automatic Weights[/k] to parent the mesh to the rig (Image 34). Go into Pose Mode (Image 35) and start playing around with the rig. On the right, go to the Data tab and enable In Front in the Viewport Display (Image 36).

Select all mesh objects and the rig, making sure the rig is the active object and [k]Ctrl-P > With Automatic Weights[/k] to parent the mesh to the rig (Image 34). Go into Pose Mode (Image 35) and start playing around with the rig. On the right, go to the Data tab and enable In Front in the Viewport Display (Image 36).

section.header: Testing the Rig and Fixing Weights
